title: QLAs – How to Use Them Well
author: Craig Latimir
summary: Craig Latimir argues that question level analyses (QLAs) -- the colourful spreadsheets showing how every student performed on every question -- are time-consuming to produce and, by themselves, largely useless, and sets out how to make them purposeful. He warns against assuming a red column means an entire topic needs reteaching without first checking the actual question and a sample of student responses, since the real cause might be a specific misconception, a complex reasoning demand, or overlap with another weak topic. Latimir recommends comparing performance against a nationally representative dataset to identify where the biggest true gaps lie, rather than simply chasing whichever columns look reddest, and argues teachers should focus reteaching on a few high-leverage areas rather than producing dozens of individualised worksheets students can't meaningfully use without one-to-one tuition. He also stresses balancing the reactive use of QLA data (addressing this class's specific gaps) with proactive curriculum changes so future cohorts don't fall into the same trap, and separating quick-win errors from substantial gaps requiring dedicated reteach time. Latimir closes by insisting teachers diagnose and fix root causes of misunderstanding rather than drilling the exact failed question, since that specific question won't reappear on a future assessment.
points: Latimir warns against assuming a red QLA column means a whole topic needs reteaching without first checking the actual question and a sample of student responses for the real cause.
He recommends benchmarking performance against a nationally representative dataset to find genuine outlier weaknesses, rather than simply chasing whichever columns look reddest on the page.

His advice explicitly rejects producing 30 individualised worksheets per class, arguing that without one-to-one tuition students can't learn effectively from model answers alone -- better to teach a few high-leverage things well.

Latimir's closing rule -- fix the root cause, not the specific failed question -- reflects a broader assessment principle: drilling the exact question that appeared once won't help since it won't reappear.
quotes: Question level analysis (big old spreadsheets which look very colourful and contain data about how every student did on every question) are time consuming to produce and, by themselves, are not useful.
When you see a big column of red under a question title, do not just assume everything about that topic needs to be retaught.
It is your job when reviewing whole class assessments to do the greatest good for the greatest number, teaching those things well is better than teaching everything poorly.
This data is going to be produced as a result of the teaching this class had. As well as being reactive in the moment to this class don’t forget to be proactive as well.
You need to diagnose the gap in their understanding and teach more holistically. That exact question won’t come up again, make sure you fix the cause, and not just the symptom.
I think QLAs can be an incredibly powerful tool but it’s important to remember that is all they are, a tool.
